# How bacteria cause damage

> *A bacterium that lives harmlessly in the colon can infect the bladder, and a sore throat that has
> cleared can be followed weeks later by damage to the heart. The tools a bacterium carries, and the
> response they provoke, decide where it can live and what harm follows.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
- Relate the tools a bacterium carries to the steps of infection it has to complete.
- Explain how adhesins and pili decide which tissue a bacterium can colonise, and when invasion is
  needed at all.
- Explain how a capsule and survival inside phagocytes defeat the defences of a tissue, and name the
  gap in host defence that each exposes.
- Distinguish exotoxins from endotoxin by structure, release, action and use in vaccines, and sort
  exotoxins by what they do to a host cell.
- Explain how superantigens, molecular mimicry and granulomas damage the host through its own
  response.
- Judge, for a given infection, whether the damage comes mainly from the bacterium or mainly from the
  host's response.
:::

## The steps of damage {#sec-bdam-steps}

Before a bacterium can damage a host it usually has to arrive at a surface, stay there and multiply.
The exception is a toxin already formed in food, as when a toxin of *Staphylococcus aureus* causes
vomiting within hours of a meal with no infection at all (see [*Gram-positive
cocci*](gram-positive-cocci.qmd#sec-gpc-aureus)). Damage is the last of the steps of infection, and
anything a bacterium uses to complete one of those steps is a virulence factor (see [*Microbes and
their hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-steps)).

::: {.flow}
1. Attach to a host surface
2. Invade the tissue, or act from the surface
3. Evade phagocytes and antibodies
4. Multiply, taking iron from the host
5. Damage cells directly or with a toxin
6. Provoke a response that damages the tissue
:::

The first four steps decide whether an infection becomes established, and the last two decide what
the patient suffers. Both sources of damage, the bacterium and the response it provokes, usually act
together (see [*Microbes and their hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-drf)).

## Getting in and staying {#sec-bdam-establish}

### Attachment and invasion {#sec-bdam-attach}

Body surfaces are swept clean. Mucus is moved by cilia and swallowed, urine flushes the bladder, and
epithelial cells are shed with whatever is stuck to them, so a bacterium that cannot hold on is
carried away. An **adhesin** is a bacterial surface molecule that binds a specific molecule on a host
cell or in the tissue around it. Many adhesins sit at the tip of a pilus (see [*How bacteria are
built and get energy*](bacteria-build-energy.qmd#sec-bact-extras)). Because an adhesin binds one kind
of molecule, attachment sets the organism's tropism, the tissues it can occupy (see [*Microbes and
their hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-steps)).

::: {.example}
The *Escherichia coli* strains that cause urinary tract infection carry pili whose adhesins bind
sugars on the cells lining the bladder, so they are held against the flow of urine instead of being
washed out (see [*Enterobacterales*](enterobacterales.qmd)).
:::

Attachment to plastic or metal works the same way. Bacteria that settle on a catheter or a
prosthetic joint build a biofilm (see [*How bacteria are built and get
energy*](bacteria-build-energy.qmd#sec-bact-extras)), in which they are sheltered from phagocytes
and harder for drugs to kill.

**Invasion** is entry through an epithelial surface into the tissue beneath, or into host cells
themselves. Some bacteria carry proteins that make an epithelial cell take them in. Many others stay
on the surface and act from it: an *E. coli* strain that causes watery diarrhoea attaches to the
cells lining the small intestine without entering them, and sends a toxin into them
([Toxins](#sec-bdam-toxins)).

Invasion is often unnecessary, because a barrier has already been broken by injury, surgery or a
device (see [*Microbes and their hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-opportunism)).

::: {.example}
*Bacteroides fragilis* lives harmlessly in the colon. When the bowel wall is breached, by perforation
or surgery, it reaches the peritoneal cavity and multiplies there (see [*Anaerobes*](anaerobes.qmd)).
:::

### Evading defences {#sec-bdam-evade}

A bacterium multiplying in tissue meets phagocytes, the cells that engulf and digest microbes. In the
surrounding fluid it meets antibodies and **complement**, a set of proteins in the blood that, once
activated on a microbe's surface, coat it for phagocytes and can assemble pores that lyse bacteria.
Antibodies coat bacteria in the same way, so that a phagocyte can grip them. Two mechanisms defeat
these defences, and each one points to a host whose defences leave it exposed.

A capsule, the polysaccharide layer outside the wall (see [*How bacteria are built and get
energy*](bacteria-build-energy.qmd#sec-bact-extras)), gives a phagocyte little to grip and buries the
surface molecules that antibodies and complement would otherwise bind. A person with asplenia,
absence of a functioning spleen, is at particular risk from encapsulated bacteria (see [*Microbes and
their hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-factors)).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Predict: why is a capsule especially dangerous in a person with asplenia? (Click to check)
A capsule resists phagocytes until antibody and complement coat it. The spleen does two things
against encapsulated bacteria in the blood: it makes much of the early antibody against capsular
polysaccharide, and blood passes through it slowly enough for its macrophages to remove bacteria
that are only lightly coated, which phagocytes elsewhere miss. Without a functioning spleen both are
lost, and encapsulated bacteria can multiply in the blood over hours.
:::

::: {.example}
The capsule of *B. fragilis* works at two steps: it resists phagocytes, and it promotes the formation
of an abscess, a walled-off collection of pus in which the bacteria continue to grow.
:::

The second mechanism is to survive the phagocyte. A phagocyte kills what it engulfs by fusing the
vesicle containing it with a lysosome, whose acid and enzymes digest the contents. *Mycobacterium
tuberculosis* prevents that fusion, so it survives and multiplies inside the macrophage that took it
up.

::: {.example}
*M. tuberculosis* inhaled into the alveoli is engulfed by alveolar macrophages and multiplies inside
them, and infected macrophages carry it to the lymph nodes of the chest (see [*Atypicals and
mycobacteria*](atypicals-mycobacteria.qmd)).
:::

A bacterium inside a host cell is out of reach of antibodies, and a drug has to enter the cell to act
on it. Its control depends instead on cell-mediated immunity, the defence by T cells against
infected cells and against organisms that live inside host cells. Intracellular bacteria therefore cause more frequent, more
severe and more widespread disease in people whose cell-mediated immunity is impaired (see [*Microbes
and their hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-factors)).

The host also withholds iron, which bacteria need in order to multiply, by keeping it bound to its
own proteins. Many bacteria secrete **siderophores**, molecules that bind iron more tightly than those
host proteins do and are then taken back into the bacterial cell (see [*Microbes and their
hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-steps)).

## Toxins {#sec-bdam-toxins}

Two different kinds of molecule are called toxins. **Exotoxins** are protein toxins secreted by
bacteria, each acting on a specific target. Endotoxin is the lipopolysaccharide (LPS) of the
Gram-negative outer membrane, a structural part of the bacterial cell rather than a secreted product
(see [*How bacteria are built and get energy*](bacteria-build-energy.qmd#sec-bact-envelope)).

Compare the two feature by feature before reading the principle.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-exotoxin-endotoxin.yml"></div>

Because exotoxins are proteins, they can be inactivated and used as toxoid vaccines (see [*Detecting
and controlling microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-prevent)). LPS cannot be
treated in this way, and the inflammation it drives accounts for much of the damage in severe
Gram-negative infection.

### Exotoxins by what they do {#sec-bdam-exotoxins}

Exotoxins are grouped by what they do to a host cell. Each acts on one target, which is why a single
toxin can produce a recognisable illness.

| Action | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Kills the cell from within | Enters the cell and stops an essential process, such as protein synthesis | A Shiga toxin, carried by some *E. coli* strains, blocks the ribosomes of the cells it enters, which then die |
| Opens a hole in the membrane | A **pore-forming toxin** inserts into the host cell membrane and opens a channel, so the cell leaks and bursts | *S. aureus* lyses red cells and neutrophils with pore-forming toxins |
| Alters cell signalling | Changes a signal inside the cell without killing it, so the cell behaves abnormally | An *E. coli* enterotoxin raises cAMP in the cells lining the small intestine, which then secrete salt and water: watery diarrhoea |
| Provokes the host's own response | A **superantigen** is a toxin that activates a large fraction of the body's T cells at once; the damage comes from what those T cells release ([damage through the host](#sec-bdam-host)) | *S. aureus* in toxic shock syndrome (fever, rash and hypotension) |

Exotoxin genes are often carried on plasmids or in prophages, so toxin production can be a property
of some strains of a species and not of others (see [*How bacteria copy themselves and
change*](bacterial-genetics.qmd#sec-gen-phage)).

### Endotoxin and sepsis {#sec-bdam-endotoxin}

Lipid A, the lipid part of LPS, binds receptors on macrophages and other cells, which release the
signals of inflammation. The response that follows has the same features whatever Gram-negative
organism provokes it: fever, dilated and leaky blood vessels, and activation of clotting. Its
strength varies, because the lipid A of some organisms, such as *B. fragilis*, is a far weaker
stimulus than that of *E. coli*. Bacteria release LPS as they divide and as they are killed, so a
large number of Gram-negative bacteria in the blood can drive this response throughout the body.

**Sepsis** is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection.
**Septic shock** is sepsis in which hypotension is so severe that the tissues are no longer
adequately perfused. Gram-positive bacteria cause sepsis as well, through components of their wall
and through toxins such as superantigens, so the clinical picture does not identify the organism.

::: {.example}
*E. coli* from an infected urinary tract can reach the blood in large numbers, and the response to
its lipid A can progress to septic shock (see [*Enterobacterales*](enterobacterales.qmd)).
:::

## Damage through the host {#sec-bdam-host}

Much of the damage in a bacterial infection is done by the host's response to the bacteria rather
than by the bacteria themselves (see [*Microbes and their
hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-drf)). Four patterns account for most of it.

The first is ordinary inflammation at the site of infection, as described in general pathology.
Neutrophils arriving in large numbers release enzymes and reactive oxygen species that digest the
tissue around them as well as the bacteria, and the debris collects as pus. Pyogenic (pus-forming)
bacteria such as *S. aureus* do much of their damage this way.

The second is a toxin that provokes the response. An ordinary immune response activates the few T
cells that recognise one antigen; a superantigen bypasses that specificity and activates T cells in
bulk. The activated T cells release a flood of cytokines, the signalling proteins that immune cells
use to coordinate inflammation, and the flood causes fever, a rash and hypotension.

::: {.example}
*S. aureus* multiplying at one site, with no bacteria in the blood, can cause toxic shock syndrome
through a superantigen alone (see [*Gram-positive cocci*](gram-positive-cocci.qmd#sec-gpc-aureus)).
:::

The third is damage after the bacteria have gone. In **molecular mimicry**, host damage is caused by
antibodies or T cells raised against a microbe cross-reacting with host tissue, because a molecule of
the microbe resembles one of the host's own.

::: {.example}
Weeks after a *Streptococcus pyogenes* throat infection has cleared, antibodies and T cells that
cross-react with heart tissue can cause rheumatic fever, inflammation of the heart, joints and other
tissues, which can scar the heart valves (see [*Gram-positive cocci*](gram-positive-cocci.qmd)).
:::

The fourth is a chronic response that damages tissue while it contains the organism. Against
bacteria that survive inside macrophages, the host walls the infected cells off in a granuloma, the
pattern of chronic inflammation met in general pathology. The granuloma stops the bacteria spreading,
and the enzymes released within it destroy the surrounding tissue.

::: {.example}
In tuberculosis of the lung, granulomas contain *M. tuberculosis* for years. A strong response
destroys lung tissue around them and can leave a cavity; a weak response, as in advanced HIV
infection, lets the bacteria spread instead.
:::

### Where the damage comes from {#sec-bdam-source}

Mechanisms of damage can be placed on a range, from damage the bacterium does itself to damage done
entirely by the response.

::: {.spectrum}
[Source of the damage]{.tree-title}

- *E. coli* strains carrying a Shiga toxin: the toxin kills host cells directly
- *S. aureus* abscess: bacterial toxins and the neutrophils that gather around them
- *M. tuberculosis*: bacterial growth and a granulomatous response, in proportions that vary with the
  host
- *S. pyogenes* rheumatic fever: cross-reacting antibodies and T cells, with no bacteria left in the
  tissue

[The bacterium]{.spectrum-end} [The host response]{.spectrum-end}
:::
